description: Sound-gap lab: pairs of Hebrew sounds that English speakers merge or misplace, with plain-English mouth instructions and word pairs. Written by lane 3 from general phonology and the research notes. NOT proofread by a native speaker; every gloss, pair and mouth cue needs review before it is called verified.

pairKinds.minimal: Words that differ only in the contrast, audibly in every tradition listed in heardIn.
pairKinds.homophone: Different spellings that are said the same in Israeli Hebrew. heardIn lists only the traditions where a speaker keeping the old distinction would pronounce them differently.
pairKinds.alternation: One root where the same letter changes sound.

gaps.title: Chet and khaf versus plain English h
gaps.englishTrap: English speakers say chet as a plain h (no scrape) or as a k, or as the ch of church. Chet, khaf (no dot) and he are three different sounds in Hebrew writing.

israeli.text: Chet and khaf (no dot) are ONE sound, a scraped ch as in loch. He is a separate, soft h.

sephardi.text: Strict Sephardi/Mizrahi reading keeps chet as a throaty pharyngeal sound, different from khaf. Most American synagogues do not do this and say both as ch.

ashkenazi.text: Chet and khaf are one sound, ch as in Bach.

american_synagogue.text: Usually ch as in Bach for both. Saying h for chet is the common slip to fix.

mouth.for: khaf / chet (Israeli, Ashkenazi, most American synagogues)
steps: Say a plain h, like fogging a mirror. Notice nothing touches anywhere.
Now lift the back of your tongue up toward the roof of your mouth, near the soft part at the back, until air has to scrape through.
The sound is the ch in Scottish loch, German Bach or the start of Chanukah said the Hebrew way. It is friction, not a k and not a church ch.
Whisper a long ha as if breathing on glasses to clean them.
Tighten the muscles low in your throat while you do it, so the air is squeezed rather than scraped near the tongue.
It is smoother than the scrape of khaf. Treat this as a listen-and-copy sound; a native speaker should model it.
A light h with no scrape. Keep it quiet: ha-ha, not kha-kha.

pairs.note: Chet against kaf WITH the dot (a k). Do not say chet as k.
Spelled differently, said the same in Israeli and Ashkenazi. Only a strict pharyngeal chet would separate them.

needsNativeSpeaker: the wording of the pharyngeal chet mouth instruction
whether American Sephardi-style congregations ever keep it

gaps.title: Aleph and ayin
gaps.englishTrap: English has neither letter as a sound. Learners either pronounce nothing (usually fine in Israel) or add a hard k, h or a long vowel. The real gap is a spelling gap: two letters, often one sound.

israeli.text: Aleph and ayin are the same: a tiny catch of the throat between vowels (the middle of uh-oh) or nothing at the start of a word.

sephardi.text: Strict Sephardi/Mizrahi keeps ayin as a pharyngeal consonant, different from aleph.

ashkenazi.text: Both silent as consonants; the vowel is just said.

american_synagogue.text: Usually silent, or a catch between vowels.

steps: Say uh-oh slowly. The little stop between uh and oh is the glottal stop.
Between two vowels (sha-AL, ma-A-seh) use that catch very lightly. At the start of a word say nothing: just begin with the vowel.
Start from ah. Tighten the muscles low in your throat as if straining to lift something heavy, and keep the voice on.
It sounds strained and slightly choked. Do not use this in everyday Israeli speech; there it can mark you as reading from a prayerbook. A native speaker should model it.

pairs.note: Aleph at the end of a word is silent; so is the ayin here, which only carries a patach in the word before it.

needsNativeSpeaker: whether the Israeli glottal catch is audible in these pairs in careful speech

gaps.title: Resh versus the English r
gaps.englishTrap: The English r (tongue pulled back, lips slightly rounded) is the biggest outsider marker in Israel (see the resh drill).

israeli.text: Back-of-the-throat r (uvular), tongue tip not involved.

sephardi.text: A tapped or rolled r made with the tongue tip, as in Spanish.

ashkenazi.text: Depends on the family: tapped or back-of-the-throat.

american_synagogue.text: Most Americans use the English r. A single tap is a better choice if the back-of-the-throat r is too hard.

steps: Keep the tip of your tongue resting behind your lower front teeth and do not move it.
Say a soft gargle, or the g in a long, lazy ghhh, but without water. Let the back of the tongue lift toward the dangling uvula.
Aim for a light buzz or breathy rub, softer than the French r in rouge. Try kar, rishon, gar.
Say butter or ladder fast in American English. The tongue tip flicks once off the ridge behind the upper teeth.
Use that single flick for the resh, with no English r colour in the vowel.

needsNativeSpeaker: how soft the Israeli uvular should sound to a learner
whether the lazy-gargle cue helps or misleads

gaps.title: Tsadi: a ts at the start of a syllable
gaps.englishTrap: English only has ts at the END of words (cats, bits). At the start of a word learners drop the t, say s or z, or put a vowel before it.

sephardi.text: ts; a few traditional communities say a plain s (needs native speaker).

american_synagogue.text: ts, written tz in English (tzedakah, Tzfat).

steps: Say cats slowly. Stop right before the a and hold the t-s at the end.
Now say it with no vowel before: ts, ts, ts. Add the vowel after it: tsa, tsi, tso.
It is one quick t+s, not z and not a separate t followed by a pause.

pairs.note: Tsadi against shin, the other letter learners swap it with.

needsNativeSpeaker: whether the plain-s communities exist as stated in sources I did not retrieve

gaps.title: Kaf (with dot) and qof
gaps.englishTrap: English speakers rarely worry about this one because both sound like k. The gap is spelling: two letters, one sound. Also Hebrew k is crisper than English k (less puff of air).

sephardi.text: Same k in most American Sephardi-style use. Some Mizrahi communities say qof further back in the throat (uvular q). Which ones was not in our sources.

steps: Say sky, not key. In sky the k has almost no puff of air. Use that k.
Do not breathe out hard after the k.
Say k, then slide the contact point back until the very back of the tongue touches the soft flap at the back of the mouth (the uvula).
It feels deeper and slightly darker than k. Native speaker needed.

pairs.note: Only a community with a back-of-the-throat qof would separate them.

needsNativeSpeaker: which communities keep a uvular qof

gaps.title: Tet and tav
gaps.englishTrap: Both are a plain t for you; the gap is spelling. Ashkenazi tav without a dot becomes s, which is its own trap (Shabbos).

sephardi.text: Same t in American Sephardi-style use. Emphatic tet survives in some traditional communities (which ones was not in our sources).

ashkenazi.text: Tet is t. Tav with a dot is t, tav without a dot is s (Shabbos).

steps: Touch the tongue tip to the ridge just behind the upper front teeth (a little farther forward than English t) and release without a big puff, as in stop.
Say t while pulling the back of the tongue down and tightening the throat, so the vowel after it sounds darker. Native speaker needed.

pairs.note: Same word. Tav without a dot is t in Israeli, s in Ashkenazi.

needsNativeSpeaker: ashkenazi spelling shabos is the usual English spelling, not a phonetic claim about every dialect

gaps.title: Samekh, sin and shin
gaps.englishTrap: Samekh and sin are both s. The gap is that one dot swaps sin and shin (sh), and learners miss the dot.

israeli.text: Samekh and sin (left dot) are both s. Shin (right dot) is sh.

ashkenazi.text: Same (Lithuanian speech historically merged shin into s as well; not in current use as a model).

steps: For s keep the tongue tip near the ridge behind the top teeth and lips relaxed: ssss.
For sh pull the tongue back a little and round the lips slightly: shhh.
Check the dot: left dot s (sin), right dot sh (shin).

gaps.title: Vav and vet versus b and w
gaps.englishTrap: English speakers say vav as w (lips round) or confuse vet with bet. Israeli vav and vet are a v with the lower lip on the upper teeth. Bet with a dot is b.

israeli.text: Vav and bet without the dot (vet) are the same v. Bet with the dot is b.

sephardi.text: Usually the same; some Mizrahi communities (e.g., Yemenite, Iraqi) say vav as w (needs native speaker).

steps: Rest your upper teeth lightly on your lower lip and hum: vvvv. Feel the buzz.
Do not round the lips; that is w.
Close both lips and release a voiced pop: b.

pairs.note: Same root: bet without the dot is v, with the dot is b. Not a minimal pair.
